opening.headline: When it's difficult to satisfy the requirements of legal, sales, and development teams on a single platform, you learn how to break down requirements and divide them into app configurations and custom builds.
body: Legal requests review of contract clauses and external sharing controls, Sales requests draft proposal creation and CRM integration, Development requests code assistance and internal API calls, HR and Finance request internal policy searches and approval workflows. It is difficult to satisfy all these diverse requirements with a single platform.

In this course, you will learn to break down requirements into smaller functional and control elements, and examine each element through three fulfillment approaches—enterprise app configurations, no-code workflows, and self-built solutions—starting with the lightest option. Then, you will follow an explanation to verify how the configuration differs by examining examples such as sales proposal automation and legal contract review.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: The department-specific requirements can be divided into parts that are satisfied by enterprise app configurations and parts that require in-house development.
It is possible to assess whether the decomposition result is valid by considering priorities and justifications.

screens.title: A platform meeting the demands of legal, sales, and development teams?
screens.lead: First, read side by side the requirements from each of your departments. Pay close attention to how different in nature the requirements are.

visual.alt: The scene where different requirements from various departments converge into a single platform box.
labels: Legal: Review of contract clauses, control over external sharing
Sales: Automatic draft creation of proposals, CRM integration
Development: code assistance, internal API calls
Human Resources & Finance: Search Internal Regulations, Approval Workflows

paragraphs: Your departments have each written down what they would like. Legal wants to review contract clauses and control documents shared externally. Sales wants to retrieve customer information and automatically generate proposal drafts. Development needs tools to assist with code writing and functionality to call internal APIs. HR and Finance want to search internal policies and integrate AI into approval workflows.

Attempting to integrate these four aspects into a single platform leads to design instability. Some requirements prioritize control, others emphasize connectivity and automation, and others necessitate direct invocation of systems within the organization.

Therefore, what is needed is to break down requirements before selecting a platform. By breaking down requirements into smaller pieces, most of these pieces will already align with the settings provided by enterprise apps, and the number of truly new components that need to be built will be surprisingly small.
The question to be answered in this class is this: which requirements can be satisfied by configuration, and which requirements must be built directly?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: When grouped by department, it appears that all components need to be built. Keep in mind that splitting them by function may yield different results.

screens.outro: Let us recall our experience of organizing requirements.

screens.title: Recalling the experience of documenting requirements in writing
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever documented departmental requirements in writing? What did that document look like?
items.answer: The requirements document typically takes the form of simply collecting sentences as spoken by departments. In this form, it is impossible to determine which requirements are specified and which require construction. In this course, sentences are broken down into functional and control items and presented in a table format with specified fulfillment methods.

items.prompt: For example, will a requirement to highlight risk clauses when uploading a contract be met by existing settings, or will a new setting need to be created?
items.answer: This one sentence contains at least three components: submitting a contract, identifying and highlighting risk clauses, and ensuring the contract does not leave the system. The first two are likely basic features of a business app, while the third relates to role-based access and app access settings. The key point is that each component may have different answers.

items.prompt: Did any of the requirements really immediately call for development?
items.answer: The judgment to develop immediately often arises because development seems the most certain option. However, development shifts the responsibility of post-creation operations and control to the team. First verifying whether settings or no-code tools can reach the solution allows achieving the same outcome with significantly less burden.

screens.outro: Then I will check actual case lists to verify what the requirements look like that are satisfied by the settings.

screens.title: Requirements satisfied by configuration: already provided by the app
screens.lead: The following is a breakdown of requirements from five departments, written as a brief note. When a highlighted section is selected, it displays an explanation of why that section matches or does not match the specification.

data.text: Requirement 1. Internal regulations want Scattered across SharePoint and Confluence, searchable from one location. Requirement 2. Want Only the sales team can use the proposal function; other teams cannot.. Requirement 3. Want The new plugin will not be usable before review.. Requirement 4. Want Invoke the internal dedicated system to check inventory stock.

marks.span: Scattered across SharePoint and Confluence, searchable from one location
marks.note: Gemini Enterprise includes connectors for business systems such as Confluence, Jira, SharePoint, and ServiceNow, and provides authorized, integrated search. Since connector setup is required, it is not built in-house.

marks.span: Only the sales team can use the proposal function; other teams cannot.
marks.note: ChatGPT Enterprise allows functionality access permissions to be bundled and assigned through custom roles (RBAC), and Claude also manages roles and groups within the administrator area. Function-level access segregation is a concern related to role configuration.

marks.span: The new plugin will not be usable before review.
marks.note: In ChatGPT Enterprise, new plugins and apps are initially disabled by default, and administrators determine whether to allow them via the Admin Console. Plugin installation and internal app access are governed separately.

marks.span: Invoke the internal dedicated system to check inventory stock
marks.note: Requirements that cannot be met even with app settings and built-in connectors indicate a need to evaluate self-built solutions. However, first verify whether these requirements can be addressed through a no-code workflow.

screens.outro: There is an intermediate zone between configuration and setup, known as no-code tools. We will now examine this further.

screens.title: No-code agents and workflows: Middle ground
screens.lead: Each item can be selected to reveal what features the Gemini Enterprise Workflow Builder offers. Note that it is a tool that bridges the gap between configuration and setup.

items.title: What tool is being used to create something?
items.body: Workflow Builder is a no-code, low-code tool within the Gemini Enterprise web app that enables creating and managing chat agents and workflows. It can be built using natural language instructions or a visual editor and connects to Google data sources as well as external data sources and tools. The goal is to automate business processes without writing code.

items.title: Who can use it?
items.body: The administrator must enable the Workflow Builder toggle in the app's feature management settings for users to use it. In other words, even no-code tools are under the administrator's control. Agents and workflows created are deployed to specific users or groups within the organization.

items.title: How does a workflow begin?
items.body: A workflow starts with a trigger and executes a series of predefined steps in order. Event triggers detect changes in connector data through polling and initiate actions. When changes such as a new email, updated schedule, or new file are detected, the configured workflow runs. It can also be set to execute repeatedly on a schedule.

items.title: Where does humanity intervene?
items.body: The human intervention stages are of two types. Request info pauses the workflow and prompts the user for additional information. Approval displays the output and requires human approval before proceeding to the next stage. In workflows where human verification is needed, such as a draft proposal, an Approval stage is included.

items.title: What to verify before deployment
items.body: Simulation is a feature that allows you to identify issues and preview behavior before enabling a workflow. A workflow can be saved as a draft or enabled to run actually, and versions can be split and managed even after it is enabled. It is safe to follow the order of first verifying via simulation and then enabling the workflow.

screens.outro: I'll summarize when it's impossible to reach even without coding, and how to determine the priority among requirements.

screens.title: Three satisfaction methods and required signals for construction
screens.lead: The following table compares three approaches that satisfy the requirements. Listed from top to bottom in order of increasing simplicity, the requirements should be examined starting from the top.

data.caption: Three ways to satisfy the requirement
rows: Search, summarization, feature access separation, app permission requirements
Role, group, connector, app allowance settings
Unified search across SharePoint and Confluence documents, sales team-specific feature access
Workflow automation with triggers and approval stages
Admin toggle, shared target, approval stage, simulation
Create a draft proposal when a new file is uploaded, then proceed after approval by the responsible party.
Internal enterprise system calls, complex orchestration, and requirements needing separate logging and evaluation frameworks
Keys, permissions, logs, and assessments are directly designed by the team.
A work tool that calls the internal inventory system to verify inventory levels
data.notes: Before deciding to implement, confirm two key aspects. First, identity. Gemini Enterprise uses an Identity Provider (IdP) to identify users and determine access permissions for search results, so identity configuration must be established first. Second, compliance certifications and security controls. Items already included in the product can be excluded from requirements. These requirements are then sorted by impact, risk, and fulfillment cost to establish a processing order. The table order reflects review sequence, not priority. Resolving requirements encountered in the upper section by addressing them in the lower section only increases unnecessary operational overhead.

screens.outro: Now, let's move on to an explanation by directly breaking down cases from two departments.

screens.title: Explanation: Automation of sales proposals and legal contract review
screens.lead: The instructor follows the process of breaking down requirements from two departments and establishing the configuration. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step. Pay attention to how the configurations differ between the two cases.

visual.alt: A diagram showing the requirements from sales and legal departments divided into a connected configuration and a controlled configuration.

steps.title: Step 1: Break down the sales requirements
steps.body: The business requirement states that a proposal draft should be automatically generated. Breaking this down reveals three components: retrieving customer information from CRM, generating the draft using the retrieved information, and the responsible person reviewing the draft. For each component, different fulfillment methods may apply, so each is described step by step.

steps.title: Step 2: Sales verifies whether it is satisfied by connection and flow.
steps.body: CRM data lookup is handled via connector, while draft creation and flow control are managed through Workflow Builder. To add manager review, simply include an Approval stage. Before deployment, observe the workflow behavior through simulation, and share it with sales groups only via the Workflow Builder toggle that is enabled by the administrator. Once this scope is complete, no custom development is required for sales requirements.

steps.title: Step 3: Break down the legal requirements
steps.body: The legal department's requirement is to review the contract without exposing it externally and to maintain records. This breaks down into three components: controlling the release of the contract outside the organization, reviewing the contract clauses, and maintaining audit records of who performed what actions. Control and documentation are the core elements, unlike in sales.

steps.title: Step 4: Legal oversees prioritizes control setup.
steps.body: The core of legal compliance lies in access permissions and application controls. Roles are defined to determine who can use the contract review functionality, and administrators restrict the allowed applications and plugins. New plugins and applications are typically disabled by default, so they are enabled only after review. If gaps remain in contract review accuracy or if separate evaluation frameworks are not fully covered—meaning certain parts of the contract are inaccessible to the application—then the configuration should be reviewed.

steps.title: Step 5: Compare the two configurations
steps.body: Comparing the two cases in a table reveals their structural differences. Sales follows a connection-and-flow-oriented architecture, linking data and establishing flows; legal affairs follows a control-and-records-oriented architecture, defining and documenting who accesses what. Both can start without any pre-built components, using only configuration and no-code capabilities, with only the remaining pieces becoming potential build candidates. This table serves as the basis for verifying the validity of the decomposition results.

screens.outro: I will conclude by summarizing the decision criteria derived from the case.

screens.title: Do not build if requirements are satisfied by configuration.
screens.lead: I will summarize what I have seen so far into one judgment standard.

paragraphs: When receiving a departmental requirement, the first step is to break it down into functional and control components. For each component, evaluate the fulfillment approach starting from the simplest option: first check if it can be met through enterprise app settings; if not, consider meeting it via no-code workflows; only if neither is possible should a custom build be selected. The principle of this sequence is that requirements satisfied by settings do not require construction.

The signal that construction is needed is relatively clear: when you need to call an internal dedicated system, when complex orchestration is required, or when separate logging and evaluation systems are needed. Conversely, integrated search, function-level access separation, app permitting, and approval-stage repetitive workflows are mostly achievable through configuration and no-code solutions.

Not every department requires the same configuration. For example, sales, where connectivity and flow are key, has different requirements than legal, where control and record-keeping are paramount. The order in which settings are determined depends on the nature of the requirements.

When multiple requests come in simultaneously, priorities are needed. By sorting them based on the scope of affected parties, the risk if the request is implemented incorrectly, and the cost of fulfilling it, you can provide a justified rationale for determining which request to address first. Do not forget that even no-code tools operate under controls such as administrator toggles and approval stages.

Finally, remember to verify whether the decomposition results are reasonable. Check that each component has a one-line justification for its fulfillment, that components classified as "construction" include a clear explanation for why they do not fall under settings or no-code options, and that priorities are explained in terms of impact, risk, and cost. Components lacking justifications are typically those that have received less scrutiny. Reviewing the decomposition table together with the department ensures easier agreement and provides a basis for future configuration changes.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The requirements are prioritized in the order of app settings, no-code workflows, and custom builds. If app settings are sufficient, no build is required.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Internal policy documents exist in SharePoint and Confluence; what's needed is an integrated search that reflects permissions. What is the most appropriate judgment?
options: Since an internal system call is required, it is built in-house immediately.
First create a no-code workflow to build the search logic directly.
Keep both the plugin and the app open and let the user choose.
Do not provision if the app settings with connector are satisfied.
checks.explain: It is principle to not build solutions that meet requirements with app settings providing integrated search reflecting permissions via connectors, such as Gemini Enterprise.

wrong.0: The requirement reached through connector search is not a self-built signal.
wrong.1: Searching is already provided by the app, so there is no need to implement new logic.
wrong.2: New plugins and apps typically require administrator approval.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes. Requirements that match the settings are not implemented.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think again. First, you need to determine whether this requirement touches upon the app's fundamental functionality.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: In a proposal workflow created using Workflow Builder, which intervention step should be used to require a responsible party to review the draft before proceeding to the next stage?
checks.explain: The human intervention stages are of two types: Request info, which receives additional information, and Approval, which proceeds after approval. To proceed after verification, Approval is required.

wrong.0: Request info is a step for receiving information, not a step that approves and advances the process.
wrong.2: A trigger is a condition that initiates a flow, not a step requiring human intervention.
wrong.3: Simulation is a feature that allows you to preview the behavior before deployment.

checks.correctFeedback: Correct. The step of verifying and proceeding is Approval.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Sorry. Consider the two types of human intervention and think about their respective uses.

glossary.def: This involves breaking down a department's requirements into smaller functions and control items, and then defining respective satisfaction methods for each.
This is a solution approach that addresses requirements using only the role, connectors, and workflow features of enterprise apps.
This is a tool that enables no-code and low-code development of agents and workflows in Gemini Enterprise.
This is a step in the workflow where a human participant is involved, such as requesting information or approving.
The result is the prioritization order of requirements based on impact scope, risk, and fulfillment cost.

misconceptions.myth: If the requirements differ, development should be started immediately.
misconceptions.fact: Breaking down the requirements shows that most components relate to app settings or no-code workflows. First verify which components are accessible, then proceed to build only the remaining ones.
The Workflow Builder can only be used after an administrator enables the feature toggle and is controlled by approval stages and shared recipients.

misconceptions.myth: All departments have the same configuration.
misconceptions.fact: Requirements where connectivity and flow are core, such as sales, differ in structure from those where control and record-keeping are core, such as legal affairs.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The requirement checks satisfaction in the order of app settings, no-code workflows, and self-built solutions.
If the settings are satisfied, no setup will be performed.
Deployment is used for requirements that apps cannot reach, such as internal system calls or complex orchestration.
Priority is determined by impact scope, risk, and cost satisfaction.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Among our requirements, what truly needs to be implemented, and what can be addressed through configuration?
